Molecular graphs

Source: vignettes/molecular-graphs.Rmd
molecular-graphs.Rmd
library(graphlearnR)

A molecule is a graph: atoms are nodes and bonds are edges. Molecular property prediction is graph classification or regression with node features (the element, charge, aromaticity) and edge features (the bond order). This article shows how to build such graphs, how to split them by scaffold so that test molecules are structurally new, and how to train an edge aware GIN.

graphlearnR does not parse SMILES strings or compute chemical scaffolds. Use a chemistry toolkit such as RDKit (in Python, or through an R interface) to get atoms, bonds and Bemis-Murcko scaffolds, and pass them to graphlearnR as plain vectors and tables.

Atoms and bonds

molecule_graph() takes element symbols and a bond table. Atoms become a one hot encoding over a list of common elements plus an “other” column; bonds become a one hot encoding of the bond order (1, 2, 3, and 1.5 for aromatic) on both directions of each bond.

# acetic acid, heavy atoms only: C-C(=O)-O
acetic <- molecule_graph(
  atoms = c("C", "C", "O", "O"),
  bonds = data.frame(from = c(1, 2, 2), to = c(2, 3, 4), order = c(1, 2, 1))
)
acetic
#> <graph_data> undirected graph: 4 nodes, 6 edges (3 undirected pairs)
#>   node features [4 x 10]
#>   edge features [6 x 4]
acetic$x[, c("C", "O", "other")]
#>      C O other
#> [1,] 1 0     0
#> [2,] 1 0     0
#> [3,] 0 1     0
#> [4,] 0 1     0
cbind(t(acetic$edge_index), acetic$edge_attr)
#>          bond_1 bond_2 bond_3 bond_1.5
#> [1,] 1 2      1      0      0        0
#> [2,] 2 1      1      0      0        0
#> [3,] 2 3      0      1      0        0
#> [4,] 3 2      0      1      0        0
#> [5,] 2 4      1      0      0        0
#> [6,] 4 2      1      0      0        0

Element and bond order vocabularies can be changed with elements and bond_orders. Further atom features (formal charge, hydrogen count) can be added by binding columns to g$x before training.

A synthetic data set

dataset_synthetic_molecules() generates small random molecules with a carbon backbone that is either a chain or a ring of five or six atoms, with random nitrogen and oxygen atoms and side chains. The label says whether the molecule has a ring. The molecules are synthetic and carry no chemical meaning; they exist to demonstrate the workflow without downloading anything.

mols <- dataset_synthetic_molecules(200, seed = 1)
labels <- vapply(mols, function(m) as.character(m$graph_y), "")
table(labels)
#> labels
#> chain  ring 
#>   113    87
scaffolds <- attr(mols, "scaffold")
head(sort(table(scaffolds), decreasing = TRUE))
#> scaffolds
#>    acyclic ring6_het3 ring5_het2 ring6_het2 ring5_het1 ring6_het1 
#>        113         18         16         11          9          7

Scaffold splits

A random split puts near copies of the same scaffold in training and test, which overstates how well a model generalizes to new chemistry. The scaffold split of MoleculeNet (Wu et al. 2018) groups molecules by scaffold, sorts the groups from largest to smallest, and fills training, then validation, then test. No scaffold appears in two parts.

sp <- split_graphs(length(mols), method = "scaffold", groups = scaffolds)
lengths(sp)
#> train   val  test 
#>   160    22    18
intersect(scaffolds[sp$train], scaffolds[sp$test])
#> character(0)
table(labels[sp$test])
#> 
#> ring 
#>   18

Because the largest group (here every acyclic molecule) goes to training, the test set of a scaffold split can have a very different label mix from training. Report the label distribution of each part along with the metrics.

Training an edge aware GIN

gnn_model("gin", edge_dim = ...) uses GINE layers, which add the bond features to each message, and sum pooling gives one vector per molecule.

library(torch)
torch_manual_seed(1)
model <- gnn_model("gin", input_dim = ncol(mols[[1]]$x), hidden_dim = 32,
                   output_dim = 2, num_layers = 3, pool = "sum",
                   edge_dim = ncol(mols[[1]]$edge_attr))
fit <- train_graph_model(model, mols[sp$train], "graph_classification",
                         val_data = mols[sp$val], epochs = 40, batch_size = 32,
                         seed = 1)
evaluate_graph_model(fit, mols[sp$test])
#>              metric      value
#> 1          accuracy 0.94444444
#> 2 balanced_accuracy 0.94444444
#> 3   precision_macro 0.50000000
#> 4      recall_macro 0.47222222
#> 5          f1_macro 0.48571429
#> 6               ece 0.12851698
#> 7             brier 0.07594893
#> 8           roc_auc         NA

For comparison, a random stratified split:

sp_r <- split_graphs(length(mols), labels = labels, seed = 1)
torch_manual_seed(1)
model_r <- gnn_model("gin", ncol(mols[[1]]$x), 32, 2, num_layers = 3, pool = "sum",
                     edge_dim = ncol(mols[[1]]$edge_attr))
fit_r <- train_graph_model(model_r, mols[sp_r$train], "graph_classification",
                           val_data = mols[sp_r$val], epochs = 40, batch_size = 32,
                           seed = 1)
evaluate_graph_model(fit_r, mols[sp_r$test])
#>              metric     value
#> 1          accuracy 0.7500000
#> 2 balanced_accuracy 0.7222222
#> 3   precision_macro 0.8437500
#> 4      recall_macro 0.7222222
#> 5          f1_macro 0.7150997
#> 6               ece 0.2657013
#> 7             brier 0.4401036
#> 8           roc_auc 1.0000000

Real data: MUTAG

MUTAG (Debnath et al. 1991) holds 188 nitroaromatic compounds labeled by mutagenicity on bacteria, distributed with the TU graph kernel benchmarks (Morris et al. 2020). graphlearnR does not ship it; download_tu_dataset() fetches the archive from the TU Dortmund site, checks its checksum, and reads it. Node labels (the element) become one hot node features and edge labels (the bond type) become edge features. The chunk below is not run when this article is built, so building the documentation never downloads data.

mutag <- download_tu_dataset("MUTAG")
mutag
graphs <- lapply(seq_along(mutag), function(i) mutag[[i]])
y <- vapply(graphs, function(g) as.character(g$graph_y), "")
sp <- split_graphs(length(graphs), labels = y, seed = 1)
torch_manual_seed(1)
model <- gnn_model("gin", ncol(graphs[[1]]$x), 64, 2, num_layers = 4, pool = "sum",
                   edge_dim = ncol(graphs[[1]]$edge_attr))
fit <- train_graph_model(model, graphs[sp$train], "graph_classification",
                         val_data = graphs[sp$val], epochs = 100, batch_size = 32,
                         early_stopping = 20, seed = 1)
evaluate_graph_model(fit, graphs[sp$test])

MUTAG is small, so test metrics vary a lot between splits. Repeat over several seeds or use cross validation and report the spread, not one number; see the evaluation article. MUTAG does not come with SMILES, so a scaffold split needs the structures from another source.

References

Debnath, A. K., Lopez de Compadre, R. L., Debnath, G., Shusterman, A. J. and Hansch, C. (1991). Structure-activity relationship of mutagenic aromatic and heteroaromatic nitro compounds. Journal of Medicinal Chemistry, 34, 786 to 797.

Morris, C., Kriege, N. M., Bause, F., Kersting, K., Mutzel, P. and Neumann, M. (2020). TUDataset: a collection of benchmark datasets for learning with graphs. ICML workshop on graph representation learning.

Wu, Z., Ramsundar, B., Feinberg, E. N. et al. (2018). MoleculeNet: a benchmark for molecular machine learning. Chemical Science, 9, 513 to 530.
